newsitem.title: USA: Northeast may seek N Hampshire rate cut bonds.
newsitem.headline: Northeast may seek N Hampshire rate cut bonds.

text.p: - Northeast Utilities unit Public Service Co. of New Hampshire said on Tuesday it might seek state-backed financing of $1 billion in stranded costs, which could lower electric rates by 10 percent as New Hampshire moves toward electric competition,
Gary Long, a vice president of Public Service, told the House Science, Technology and Energy Committee that "the potential is to securitize more than $1 billion" in stranded costs.
As a rule of thumb, Long said, company rate specialists figured each $100 million in financing could yield an average rate reduction of one percent.

New Hampshire is a leader in the movement to abolish the traditional monopoly territories for public utilities and allow competition for electric customers as a way to reduce some of the nation's highest electricity bills. The Public Utilities Commission is expected to issue an interim order on the move to competition on Feb. 28.

A major sticking point is how to handle stranded costs, the investments in generating plants and other items that utilities made to serve their monopoly areas that cannot be recovered if rates are competitive.

The committee is considering a bill to finance these costs through state-issued bonds. Under the bill debated Tuesday, utilities could use the bonds to finance stranded costs and other expenses such as mandated environmental expenditures and buyouts of small power producer contracts. Ratepayers in the utility's old franchise area would be obliged to repay the bonds in addition to their current electric bills.

Curtis Probst, a vice president at Salomon Bros., said such securities could carry a top-ranked AAA rating because they would have dedicated revenues, mandated by the state. The state's general obligation bonds carry an Aa rating from Moody's Investors Services and AA+ from Standard & Poor's.
Most witnesses at the hearing were generally supportive and the bil should come up for House action in the next couple of weeks.

Robert Backus, president of the Campaign for Ratepayers' Rights, said this represented a change in the state's utility policy. In the past, Backus said, the state had guaraneed rates but not revenues. This bill would guarantee revenues to the utilities.

In Connecticut, the state attorney general last week opposed a proposal by Northeast Utililtes to refinance up to $3 billion of stranded costs through issuance of rate-reduction bonds. ((--Boston bureau, 617-367-4106))
